 Use tab to navigate through the menu items. Randy Travis Opens the Vault and Gives Country Music Something Worth Holding Onto with ‘Same Old Way’
 All Country News 4 minutes ago 3 min read Twelve previously unreleased recordings reunite fans with an irreplaceable voice, adding another chapter to a legacy that continues to grow. Some voices become part of country music’s history. Randy Travis’s became part of its identity. 
 That deep, unmistakable baritone could make a confession feel personal, a heartbreak feel permanent and an ordinary moment feel worth a song. With Same Old Way , out now, fans have 12 more reasons to remember why his place in country music is secure. 
 His first album of previously unreleased material in more than 18 years, the collection draws from recordings made between 1986 and 2013. Longtime producer and collaborator Kyle Lehning unearthed the songs, then assembled, remixed and remastered them with Travis’s input. The result brings a previously unheard stretch of his recording history into the light. 
 The circumstances give this release considerable emotional weight. Following Travis’s 2013 stroke, the prospect of another album like this carried an uncertainty that longtime fans understood all too well. These recordings offer another opportunity to connect with the singer whose work has soundtracked their marriages, breakups, Sunday drives and everyday lives. 
 Lehning’s involvement matters. As Travis’s longtime producer, he brings an understanding of the artist behind the recordings. Preserving that relationship—and giving Travis a voice in how these songs reach listeners—makes this project especially meaningful. 
 Three tracks offer particularly compelling entry points. 
 “Fish On” brings the personality. Written by Travis and Ron Avis, the song celebrates his longtime love of fishing, finding its pleasure in getting out on the water and seeing what bites. Its easygoing premise offers a welcome reminder of the humor and everyday warmth that belong in Travis’s musical world alongside the heartache. Country music has always made room for small pleasures. A fishing pole and somewhere to cast it are plenty to build a song around. 
 “I Don’t Care” heads straight for the emotional wreckage. Co-written with Michael Curtis, it follows a relationship fractured by betrayal, reaching the point where apologies can no longer repair the damage. The title’s bluntness is the hook: those three words carry the exhaustion of someone who has already spent too much energy hurting. It is fertile ground for the direct, deeply human storytelling that has long defined Travis’s appeal. 
 The title track, “Same Old Way,” gives the collection its emotional anchor. Its narrator remains caught in the daily repetition of missing someone, unable to find relief in distractions or his friends’ assurances that time will help. That familiar country predicament gains another layer through its songwriting credit: Travis and Lehning wrote the song together, their only shared composition. On an album made possible by their enduring collaboration, that detail carries real significance. 
 Together, those songs capture three essential ingredients in Travis’s appeal: warmth, wounded honesty and an ability to give familiar experiences lasting resonance. 
 The larger story of Same Old Way is one of rediscovery. A vault release can reveal the creative decisions and unfinished business behind a celebrated catalog. Here, it gives listeners access to songs that waited years for their moment, and gives an artist with an extraordinary history more music to share. 
 There is something powerful about that opportunity. Fans know the hits. They know where the choruses land and which lines still catch them off guard. Now, they get to experience the pleasure of discovery again. 
 For an artist whose voice has become so familiar, another first listen is a remarkable gift. Randy Travis has already given country music songs that will outlive generations. With Same Old Way, he gives listeners something they could not take for granted: another chapter.
